summary: Defines Structure of Management Information Version 2 (SMIv2), the adapted subset of the ASN.1 notation used to describe MIB modules, and assigns a set of administrative values. It is an Internet Standard. It obsoletes RFC 1902.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2578 sets the writing rules for MIB modules in SNMP. It says how to describe each object a device can report or control, what data type it holds, and how alerts are defined, so every tool reads the same descriptions the same way.

subtitle: The rules for writing MIB modules: how to describe managed objects, notifications and their data types.

tldr.problem: SNMP management information must be written so that any system can parse and understand it, which needs exact rules for defining objects, types and notifications.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2578 defines SMIv2, an adapted subset of ASN.1 plus the MODULE-IDENTITY, OBJECT-IDENTITY, OBJECT-TYPE and NOTIFICATION-TYPE macros used to write MIB modules.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard (STD 58) that obsoletes RFC 1902 and provides the shared grammar for all SMIv2 MIB modules.

today: RFC 2578 is an Internet Standard (STD 58) and has not been obsoleted. It obsoleted RFC 1902 and works with RFC 2579 and RFC 2580.

sections.title: Purpose of SMIv2
sections.content:
Management information is a collection of managed objects in a Management Information Base (MIB). Related objects are grouped into MIB modules, written using an adapted subset of ASN.1 (1988). The Structure of Management Information (SMI) defines that subset and the associated administrative values.

The SMI has three parts: module definitions (the MODULE-IDENTITY macro), object definitions (the OBJECT-TYPE macro) and notification definitions (the NOTIFICATION-TYPE macro). The original SMI is called SMI version 1 (SMIv1); this revision is SMI version 2 (SMIv2).
sections.plainLanguage: A MIB is a catalogue of things a device can report or control. SMIv2 is the grammar for writing that catalogue, so that any management tool can read it correctly.

sections.title: The SNMPv2-SMI Module
sections.content:
The RFC itself defines an information module, SNMPv2-SMI. It declares the root of the naming tree with object identifiers such as org, dod and internet, and standard branches such as mgmt, mib-2, experimental, private, enterprises, security and snmpV2. It also defines the EXTENDED UTCTime format, which allows four-digit years.

The allowed syntax for objects is ObjectSyntax, a choice of three built-in ASN.1 types (INTEGER, OCTET STRING, OBJECT IDENTIFIER) and eight application-defined types: Integer32, IpAddress, Counter32, Gauge32, Unsigned32, TimeTicks, Opaque and Counter64.
sections.plainLanguage: SMIv2 comes with the base naming tree that all MIBs hang from, plus a fixed list of data types an object may use, such as counters and addresses.

sections.title: Information Modules and Macros
sections.content:
An information module is an ASN.1 module that defines network-management information. There are three typical kinds: MIB modules (which use OBJECT-TYPE and NOTIFICATION-TYPE), compliance statements for MIB modules (MODULE-COMPLIANCE and OBJECT-GROUP), and capability statements for agents (AGENT-CAPABILITIES). The macros for compliance and capabilities are defined in RFC 2580.

Every information module starts with exactly one MODULE-IDENTITY invocation, immediately after any IMPORTs. It gives contact information and a revision history. Only a restricted set of ASN.1 constructs is allowed; new macros must not be defined and SMIv1 macros must not be used. The names of standard modules must be unique.
sections.plainLanguage: A module is one file of definitions. It opens with a header that names its maintainer and records each revision, and it may use only the constructs SMIv2 permits.

sections.title: Naming and Values
sections.content:
Each macro invocation appears as a descriptor, the macro name, its clauses and a value. An object name or notification name is an OBJECT IDENTIFIER. Object types are identified by an OID, and a specific object instance is named by appending instance identification to the object type's OID.

The RFC defines the rules for assigning object identifiers and the special value zeroDotZero used for null identifiers. It also specifies how values of the defined types are written.
sections.plainLanguage: Every object has a unique number, like a street address for one piece of data. A specific reading (an instance) adds its index to that number.

sections.title: The OBJECT-TYPE Macro
sections.content:
The OBJECT-TYPE macro describes a managed object. Its clauses include SYNTAX (the object's data type), MAX-ACCESS, STATUS, DESCRIPTION, and for table rows an INDEX (and optionally AUGMENTS).

MAX-ACCESS is one of not-accessible, accessible-for-notify, read-only, read-write or read-create. STATUS is one of current, deprecated or obsolete. Conceptual tables and rows are defined with SEQUENCE types and OBJECT-TYPE definitions; the INDEX clause lists the objects whose values identify each row.
sections.plainLanguage: Each object is defined in a template. The template states its data type, who may read or write it, whether it is still current, and, for a table, which values pick out each row.

sections.title: Notifications
sections.content:
The NOTIFICATION-TYPE macro defines an unsolicited transmission of management information, i.e., the contents of a SNMPv2-Trap-PDU or InformRequest-PDU. Its clauses include OBJECTS (the ordered objects that carry the information), STATUS and DESCRIPTION.

Each object named in the OBJECTS clause must have one instance present, in the given order, in every notification; the DESCRIPTION must explain the meaning of each object and say how its instance is identified. An agent may append extra objects after those named.
sections.plainLanguage: A notification is an alert sent to a manager. This macro names the objects that carry the alert's details and explains what each one means.

sections.title: Extending and Refining a Module
sections.content:
Section 9 covers refined syntax: a module may reuse a type defined elsewhere and restrict it, for example by narrowing a range or size, as long as the meaning is not changed. Section 10 covers revising a module in place. Any change with the potential to cause interoperability problems on the wire is not allowed.

When a module is revised, its MODULE-IDENTITY invocation must be updated with a new LAST-UPDATED value and a new REVISION/DESCRIPTION pair. Module names must not change and definitions must not move between modules. Obsolete definitions must not be removed, and their object identifiers must never be reassigned.

Within those limits, an object definition may be revised by, for example, adding enumerations, replacing a SYNTAX with an equivalent textual convention, changing STATUS to deprecated or obsolete, or adding DEFVAL, REFERENCE or UNITS clauses. A conceptual row may be extended by appending new columns. A notification definition may have its REFERENCE, STATUS or DESCRIPTION revised.
sections.plainLanguage: Modules can grow and be corrected over time. A module may restrict a type it borrowed from another module, and revisions must be recorded in the header. Names and numbers are never reused, and obsolete definitions stay in place.
